To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have developed a general strategy to design DNA aptamers that report target binding by changing their structures and we have isolated DNA enzymes that exhibit synchronized catalysis-signalling capabilities.

we have developed new strategies for engineering structure-switching signaling aptamers and synchronized catalysis-signalling DNA enzymes that are potentially useful for detection-directed applications.

1) structure-switching signaling aptamers are designed to report target binding by structure switching from DNA/DNA double-strand to DNA/target complex; 2) a synchronized catalysis- signaling DNA enzyme is selected that can cleave an RNA/DNA chimera substrate and report cleavage activity by fluorescence change; and 3) these two types of signaling molecules have the potential to be used in detection-directed applications
In summary, our research is concerned with
the engineering of DNA aptamers, DNA enzymes and their derivatives with fluorescence-signaling ability.
the design and development of new DNA aptamers, DNA enzymes, and DNA-based biosensors.
the development of new DNA aptamer and DNA enzyme technologies that can be applied for the detection of small molecules and proteins in complex samples.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
DNA aptamers, DNA enzymes, and their derivatives are versatile molecular tools that can be engineered for many innovative applications in molecular biology, bioengineering, and biotechnology.
DNA aptamers, DNA enzymes, and their variants with fluorescence-signaling capabilities have been developed and their applications in biosensing and molecular imaging are promising.
fluorescence-signaling DNA molecules, especially DNA aptamers, are promising tools for the development of novel biosensors and other detection-directed applications.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed new classes of signaling DNA molecules that can be widely used for detection-directed applications in the fields of chemical and biological analysis.

we have successfully demonstrated the feasibility of engineering DNA aptamers, DNA enzymes, and DNAzymes with fluorescence-signaling capabilities, which can be used as novel molecular tools for the detection of various targets.

the fluorescence-signaling DNA molecules developed in our laboratory are not just a new class of molecular tools for the study of nucleic acids, but also have the potential of providing a new generation of molecular tools that can be used in the detection-directed applications of nucleic acids.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the fluorescence-signaling properties can be readily engineered into DNA aptamers as well as DNA enzymes, thus expanding the utility of DNA aptamers from a simple binding molecule to a more complex sensing molecule and of DNA enzymes from a simple catalytic molecule to a more versatile sensing molecule.
fluorescence-signaling DNA molecules can be engineered with desired properties by combining the rational design approach with the in vitro selection technique.
fluorescence-signaling aptamers and enzymes, when combined with the latest fluorescence technologies, can serve as powerful molecular tools for detection-directed applications.
